title: Consider adding 0-hop compatibility with Meshtastic nodes
body:
Hi,

It looks like MeshCore is gaining traction and more people are switching to it. However, since people may choose to stick with Meshtastic for one reason or another, it made me think that it could be an idea to talk about whether or not it's possible to add basic communication with Meshtastic nodes. 

The use-case would be particularly relevant when traveling and so when it'd be cool to meet new people running other Lora nodes. At the moment, MeshCore and Meshtastic devices won't see each other nor will be able to talk, which means that for maximum reach one would need to have two devices running both projects. What about adding a very basic interoperability with Meshtastic to help with this aspect?

I would imagine it as MeshCore implementing only the logic around NodeInfo advertisements and the ones for receiving and sending DMs. This would work _exclusively_ for 0-hop nodes, so for other Meshtastic users that are nearby. There would be no routing or anything beyond this minimal integration of a few packet types and, in turn, MeshCore users will still keep the benefits of running Meshcore.

Now, MeshCore was born because of a few reasons, so perhaps this idea of providing compatibility might be unwanted or even not easy to technically implement or maintain over time. Mine is just a suggestion, really.
author: randshell

comments.body: I'll add my opinion: no way, don't add anything that links Meshcore to Meshtastic - never. People using Meshtastic are looking for a completely different thing. They don't want functional communication, but just looking for as many nodes as possible. It would be counterproductive to lure these users into MeshCore. MeshCore is not for gadgets, MeshCore is for real off-grid communication.

author: fdlamotte

comments.body:
Adding some ideas here regarding LED status blink strategy:

Four blink "positions" that are cycled through every n seconds:

1) BLE Connection to App status (connected or disconnected)
2) GPS fix/lock (fix or no fix)
3) Battery State of Charge (SoC) (greater than or less than a specific threshold, sell app section below)
4) New Message(s) (a new message has been received since the since the app was last viewed - this may be challenging to determine)

The theory here is that a short blink is normal/good - while a longer blink is “hey something needs to be addressed." I'm thinking that maybe a 100ms (as short as reasonably possible) for short blinks, 500ms for long blinks, with a 250ms interval between positions. A short blink should be subtle and unobtrusive.

Charging would be 0-100% LED ramp up/down every 3 seconds, with the four blink codes doing their thing every  every third charging indicator ramp up/down cycle.

When fully charged (100% State of Charge) and connected to power, LED is on continuous at 50% brightness.

In the app(s), if companion BLE device is a t1000e:

1) Display (un-dim/gray out) a toggle for mute buzzer.
2) Display (un-dim/gray out) toggle for LED indicator status lights.
3) Display cheat sheet for blink codes somewhere in the app.
(MAYBE) 4) Display a slider for battery threshold the status LED will display a "long" blink for to indicate an issue.  I think 30% SoC is a reasonable default, but some people may want notice sooner (50% SoC) or later (10% SoC) that the battery is going flat.

Some examples:

A "short long short short" would indicate the T1000e is connected to an app via BLE, DOESN'T have a gps fix, battery is OK and no new messages.

A " short short long short" would indicate an app is connected via BLE, has a GPS fix, battery is BELOW the "good" threshold, and there are no new messages.

title: add new commands to companion firmware to import and export identity
body:
This PR adds two new commands to import and export the main identity private key in the Companion Radio firmware.

`CMD_EXPORT_PRIVATE_KEY`: `23`
`CMD_IMPORT_PRIVATE_KEY`: `24`
`RESP_CODE_PRIVATE_KEY` : `14`

- `CMD_EXPORT_PRIVATE_KEY` replies with `RESP_CODE_PRIVATE_KEY` containing the 64 byte main identity key.
- `CMD_IMPORT_PRIVATE_KEY` accepts a 64 byte private key which is loaded and saved as the main identity key.

Could possibly be renamed to `CMD_EXPORT_IDENTITY_PRIVATE_KEY`, but naming is internal only...

I opted to leave out the public key from the export, as the firmware can derive it from the private key on import.
author: liamcottle

comments.body: Am a bit worried about this one. Could open an exploit where private keys could just silently get lifted off devices without the user knowing.

Yep, fair enough!

I've added the below build flags to enable/disable this feature as discussed elsewhere:

- `-D ENABLE_PRIVATE_KEY_EXPORT 1`
- `-D ENABLE_PRIVATE_KEY_IMPORT 1`

By default, these are both set to `0`, in which case the radio will reply with `RESP_CODE_DISABLED`.

title: Update README.md
body:
Your readme.md could be enriched. Please QA this!:

MeshCore

MeshCore is a lightweight, portable C++ library that enables multi-hop packet routing for embedded projects using LoRa and other packet radios. It is designed for developers who want to create resilient, decentralized communication networks that work without the internet.

🔍 What is MeshCore?

MeshCore now supports Heltec V3 LoRa devices, allowing for easy flashing without the need to compile firmware manually. Users can flash a pre-built binary using tools like Adafruit ESPTool and interact with the network through a serial console.
MeshCore provides the ability to create wireless mesh networks, similar to Meshtastic and Reticulum but with a focus on lightweight multi-hop packet routing for embedded projects. Unlike Meshtastic, which is tailored for casual and tactical LoRa communication, or Reticulum, which offers advanced encrypted networking, MeshCore balances simplicity with scalability, making it ideal for custom embedded solutions., where devices (nodes) can communicate over long distances by relaying messages through intermediate nodes. This is especially useful in off-grid, emergency, or tactical situations where traditional communication infrastructure is unavailable.

⚡ Key Features

✔️ Multi-Hop Packet Routing – Devices can forward messages across multiple nodes, extending range beyond a single radio's reach. MeshCore supports up to a configurable number of hops to balance network efficiency and prevent excessive traffic.
✔️ Supports LoRa Radios – Works with Heltec, RAK Wireless, and other LoRa-based hardware.
✔️ Decentralized & Resilient – No central server or internet required; the network is self-healing.
✔️ Low Power Consumption – Ideal for battery-powered or solar-powered devices.
✔️ Simple to Deploy – Pre-built example applications make it easy to get started.

🎯 What Can You Use MeshCore For?

- Off-Grid Communication: Stay connected even in remote areas.
- Emergency Response & Disaster Recovery: Set up instant networks where infrastructure is down.
- Outdoor Activities: Hiking, camping, and adventure racing communication.
- Tactical & Security Applications: Military, law enforcement, and private security use cases.
- IoT & Sensor Networks: Collect data from remote sensors and relay it back to a central location.

🚀 How to Get Started
- Flash the Firmware: Download the pre-built firmware binary for Heltec V3 and flash it using Adafruit ESPTool.
- Install PlatformIO in Visual Studio Code (optional for developers who want to modify the firmware).
- Download & Open the MeshCore repository.
- Select a Sample Application: Choose from chat, ping, repeater, or admin test tools.
- Monitor & Communicate using a serial console (e.g., Serial USB Terminal on Android).
- Install PlatformIO in Visual Studio Code.
- Download & Open the MeshCore repository.
- Select a Sample Application: Choose from chat, ping, repeater, or admin test tools.
- Build & Upload the firmware to your LoRa device.
- Monitor & Communicate using the serial interface.

📁 Included Example Applications
📡 Chat Applications: Secure text communication between devices.
📡 Ping Server & Client: Basic message exchange to test network connectivity.
📡 Simple Repeater: Extends network coverage by relaying messages.
📡 Test Admin: Monitors and manages repeaters remotely.
📡 Clock Synchronization: Allows nodes to sync time from GPS-enabled devices for better network stability.
